title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
hook: a man hangs upside down in a well, a serpent below, an elephant above, and he reaches for a drop of honey

segments.voice: Yesterday the night book, Sauptika, ended by the Ganga, with two sages between the weapons and a jewel carried home to Draupadi. Did you get to say a calm word? Today, the book of the women. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

A traveler is lost in a thick forest full of wild animals. Running from them, he falls into a well, but he doesn't hit the bottom. He's caught by creepers and hangs there, upside down. Below him, at the bottom of the well, waits a great serpent. Above him, at the well's mouth, stands a dark elephant. Rats are gnawing at the roots of the tree that holds the creepers. And from a honeycomb in the branches, a drop of honey falls toward his mouth. Today, the start of Stri, the book of the women, where Vidura tells this story to a grieving king.
screen: `A MAN HANGS IN A WELL.` → `A SERPENT BELOW.` → `A DROP OF HONEY.`

segments.voice: The war is over. In Hastinapura, the old blind king Dhritarashtra has heard that Duryodhana and his brothers are dead, and he falls to the ground in grief. His half-brother Vidura, the wise one who warned him again and again, sits with him. And instead of an argument, Vidura tells a story: the man in the well. In Ganguli's telling, what does the man do, hanging there between the serpent and the elephant, with the rats chewing the roots? He drinks the honey. And he wants more. He still wishes to live, and he still wants the sweetness. Then Vidura explains. The forest is the world we wander in. The wild animals are illnesses. The well is the body. The serpent at the bottom is Time, which takes everything. The elephant is the year, the rats are the days and the nights eating away at our time, and the creepers are the hope of life that holds us. The honey is the pleasures we keep reaching for, even here. Vidura isn't mocking the man. He's describing everyone, the king included. And his counsel to Dhritarashtra is gentle and hard at once: every living being comes to this; grief cannot bring your sons back; let the wise not be swept away by it. It's a strange way to open a book of mourning. Before the women walk out onto the field to find their dead, the story pauses on a man in a well, still tasting the honey.
screen: `THE KING HEARS THE NEWS` · `VIDURA TELLS A STORY` · `HE STILL WANTS THE HONEY` · then, large: `THE WELL IS THE WORLD`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and notice the breath going in and out by itself. The story counts time in days and nights. This breath is part of today, and it's here now. Breathe in, and notice one sweet thing in this moment: warmth, light, a sound, the chair holding you. Breathe out, and let it be enough. Then let the next breath come, and notice another. If you pray, you can give thanks in your prayer for this one breath. The bell holds the time.
Stri. The book of the women begins with a grieving king and Vidura's story of a man in a well, still reaching for the honey.
Your line: still reaching for the honey. Today, when you notice yourself reaching for the next sweet thing, pause and taste the one you have. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Vidura's parable of the man in the well is retold in Hindu teaching and storytelling as a picture of life held between time and desire.

original.note: woman: the name of the book of the Mahabharata where the women mourn the war's dead.

trapdoor: what you thought: the book of the women begins with the women on the battlefield.
what it means: it opens with a grieving king and Vidura's story of the man in the well.
what a scholar hears: before the mourning, the epic sets the war inside a picture of all life, so every grief to come is read through the well.
